rationale: The Aave v3 fork priced wrapped xStock collateral from an ERC4626 convertToAssets rate that a direct donation of the underlying could inflate within one transaction. The price source behind AaveOracle (not among the recovered sources) is the real defect, and none of the Slither findings touch that valuation.

FleetCommander computes NAV as the live sum of each ark's totalAssets with no donation or deviation guard, and one ark held Silo vault shares that counted depegged xUSD at par. The attacker deposited, donated cheaply acquired vgUSDC into the empty ark to inflate NAV, then redeemed; the reentrancy and timestamp findings are unrelated.

An abandoned GovernorAlpha with a low 200k quorum and voting weight that could be bought cheaply on the market controlled the Upgrader (the ProxyAdmin). One self-funded proposal handed admin to the attacker, who upgraded the service proxy and swept its reserve; the Governor implementation source was not recovered (only the proxy), so no finding covers the defect.

The permissionless launch() forwards caller-supplied initCalldata and modifyCalldata unchecked into the V4 PositionManager multicall, executed as the factory that holds every launch's LP NFT. Injecting setApprovalForAll gave the attacker operator rights to burn other users' positions; Slither's arbitrary-send-eth flags only the dust ETH refund, not this calldata forwarding.

ethFromDefund prices a redemption from the arithmetic mean of the starting and estimated ending FUM sell prices, and each call also shrinks the stored price state, so splitting one redemption into many slices pays more ETH than a single redemption. A large fund followed by 64 small defunds returned more ETH than went in; the divide-before-multiply hits are in other functions and do not describe this path dependence.

The vault values its Uniswap V3 position for permissionless mint and burn from the pool's instantaneous slot0 price, and its TWAP check guards only the manager's rebalance. An attacker skewed the tick, minted, partly restored the price and burned for a richer token mix; only the EIP173 proxy source was analyzed, so no finding applies.

The Aragon voting token wrapped the vault's own shares, and almost none were wrapped, so a single depositor who wrapped about one share held a voting majority and passed a proposal that redirected the vault's debt to an attacker strategy. The drained vault is a Yearn V3 Vyper contract and no source was recovered for any candidate, so I treat it as out of the Solidity v1 scope.

The contract registries behind Enjin's ERC-1155 adapter clones exposed an unprotected initialize that let anyone become manager and register new delegatecall bodies for the clones. The attacker installed code that moved items out of holders without approval and melted them for their ENJ backing; the registries and platform have no recovered verified source, so the incident is out of scope.

Ajna's oracle-free liquidations price bucket and auction takes only from pool-internal state, so an attacker controlling both the liquidated borrower and the taker's bucket deposit recovered almost all of the collateral for a small quote payment, at other lenders' expense. The pool clone's ERC20Pool implementation source was not recovered and no official post-mortem was found, so the exact defective accounting line is uncertain.

After swaps squeezed the WBTC reserve down to a few satoshi, calcSingleInGivenPoolOut rounded the WBTC needed for a large BPT mint down to one satoshi, and joinswapPoolAmountOut has no minimum-input or relative-error check. Repeated join and exit cycles collected almost all of the BPT supply for dust, which exitPool redeemed; the reentrancy and event findings are unrelated.
